chapters.title: Chapter 4: Beyond Black-Scholes: Extensions of the Toolkit

lessons.title: Stochastic Volatility: Why Constant Sigma Breaks Down

children.text: A trader on Rohan's desk pulls up a live Nifty options chain and asks a question the Black-Scholes formula cannot answer on its own: "If σ is one constant number, why does inverting the formula on real market prices give a different σ for every strike?" Every lesson so far has flagged constant volatility as an assumption, an idealization the previous lesson's Chapter 3 assumption table listed openly. This lesson finally opens that assumption up and looks at what breaks, and what replaces it, when volatility is allowed to move on its own.

body.text: Real option prices, inverted through the Black-Scholes formula, produce a different implied volatility at every strike, a pattern called the volatility smile or skew, direct empirical proof that constant volatility is only an approximation. Stochastic volatility models fix this by making variance itself a second stochastic process, correlated with the stock's own randomness, using exactly the multivariate Ito tools from the previous lesson.

children.text: The Empirical Problem: Implied Volatility Isn't Flat

markDefs.definition: The single value of σ that, plugged into the Black-Scholes formula alongside the option's actual known S, K, r, and τ, reproduces the option's real, observed market price exactly.

children.text: Given a real, traded option price, define its

: the σ value that makes the Black-Scholes formula output that exact market price, everything else held fixed. India VIX is precisely this quantity, aggregated across a basket of near-the-money Nifty options. If Black-Scholes's constant-σ assumption were literally true, every option on the same stock, at the same expiry, would imply the identical σ, regardless of strike.

body.caption: An illustrative Nifty options implied volatility skew (Nifty spot ≈ 24,000)

body.text: This downward-sloping pattern, called a volatility skew, is a real, persistent feature of equity index options, including Nifty and Bank Nifty, not a data artifact. Lower strikes (protective, out-of-the-money puts) consistently trade at higher implied volatility than higher strikes, reflecting real demand for crash protection. A single constant σ cannot reproduce this shape; it can only match one strike at a time.

children.text: Modeling Variance as Its Own Stochastic Process

The most influential fix, the Heston model (1993), stops treating variance as a fixed number and instead models it as v(t), a second stochastic process, correlated with the stock's own Brownian motion using exactly the two-process framework from the previous lesson. Variance is given its own SDE, one that pulls it back toward a long-run average, exactly the same mean-reverting square-root form used in interest rate modeling (the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model), an interesting cross-field reuse of the same mathematical object.

body.latex: dS = \mu S\, dt + \sqrt{v(t)}\, S\, dW_1, \qquad dv = \kappa(\theta - v)\, dt + \xi \sqrt{v}\, dW_2, \qquad dW_1\, dW_2 = \rho\, dt
body.caption: The Heston stochastic volatility model
The four new parameters the Heston model introduces

cells: Mean-reversion speed: how quickly v(t) is pulled back toward its long-run level, θ
Long-run variance level; √θ is the long-run volatility v(t) reverts toward over time
Volatility of volatility: how much v(t) itself fluctuates around its mean-reverting path
Correlation between the stock's and the variance's Brownian motions; typically negative for equities

body.text: A negative ρ here is called the leverage effect: when the stock falls, volatility tends to rise, and vice versa, exactly the well-documented inverse relationship between Nifty and India VIX. On days Nifty drops sharply, India VIX almost always spikes; on calm, rising days, it typically drifts lower. The Heston model builds this real empirical pattern directly into its correlation parameter, something a single constant σ has no way to express at all.

children.text: Simulating v(t) needs one numerical safeguard the previous chapters never had to worry about: naive Euler-Maruyama can push v below zero, since nothing in a straightforward discretization stops it, even though a real variance can never be negative. The standard fix, called full truncation, replaces v with max(v, 0) wherever it appears inside a square root.

body.caption: Simulating the Heston model with a full-truncation scheme
body.code:
import numpy as np

S0, mu = 3900, 0.15
v0, kappa, theta, xi, rho = 0.04, 2.0, 0.09, 0.3, -0.6
T, n_steps = 1.0, 252
dt = T / n_steps

S, v = np.zeros(n_steps+1), np.zeros(n_steps+1)
S[0], v[0] = S0, v0

for i in range(n_steps):
    v_pos = max(v[i], 0)  # full truncation: never take sqrt of a negative variance
    Z1 = np.random.normal(0, 1)
    Z2 = rho*Z1 + np.sqrt(1 - rho**2)*np.random.normal(0, 1)
    S[i+1] = S[i] * np.exp((mu - 0.5*v_pos)*dt + np.sqrt(v_pos*dt)*Z1)
    v[i+1] = v[i] + kappa*(theta - v_pos)*dt + xi*np.sqrt(v_pos*dt)*Z2

print(f"Initial volatility: {np.sqrt(v0):.1%}")
print(f"Final volatility:   {np.sqrt(max(v[-1], 0)):.1%}")
print(f"Long-run volatility (theta): {np.sqrt(theta):.1%}")

body.title: One simulated path of instantaneous volatility, √v(t), mean-reverting toward 30%

body.text: Pricing options under the Heston model rigorously requires solving a more complex PDE than Black-Scholes's, typically via characteristic functions and Fourier inversion, mathematical machinery well beyond this course's scope. This lesson's goal is narrower and more honest: understand precisely which assumption stochastic volatility relaxes, why it matters empirically, and how to simulate it, not to derive its full closed-form (or semi-closed-form) pricing formula.

body.title: Explain the leverage effect's sign
body.question: Why is ρ, the correlation between the stock's and variance's Brownian motions, typically calibrated to a negative value for equity indices like Nifty?
options: Because stock prices and volatility are mathematically required to always move oppositely
Because it captures the empirically observed leverage effect: sharp price declines tend to coincide with rising volatility, and calm, rising markets with falling volatility
Because a negative ρ is needed purely to keep v(t) from going negative in simulation
Because r is usually smaller than μ, forcing ρ negative
body.explanation: The negative correlation is a calibration choice that matches a real, well-documented market pattern, the inverse relationship between Nifty and India VIX, not a mathematical requirement of the model. Full truncation, not the sign of ρ, is what keeps v(t) non-negative in simulation.

body.title: Compute the long-run volatility
body.prompt: For this lesson's calibration, θ = 0.09. What is the long-run volatility, √θ, expressed as a percentage?
body.explanation: √0.09 = 0.30, or 30%. Variance, not volatility, is the quantity that mean-reverts directly in the Heston SDE; volatility is its square root, so θ itself is a variance level, not a volatility level.

cards.definition: The σ value that, plugged into the Black-Scholes formula, reproduces an option's actual observed market price; India VIX is an aggregated implied volatility measure.
The pattern where implied volatility varies systematically with strike price, direct empirical evidence against the Black-Scholes constant-volatility assumption.
A stochastic volatility model where variance v(t) follows its own mean-reverting SDE, correlated with the stock's Brownian motion via a leverage parameter ρ.
The empirical tendency for volatility to rise when prices fall and fall when prices rise, modeled in Heston via a negative correlation, ρ, between the two Brownian motions.

points: Implied volatility, the σ that makes Black-Scholes match a real market price, varies systematically with strike in real Nifty and Bank Nifty options, a pattern called the volatility smile or skew, direct evidence against constant σ.

The Heston model replaces constant σ with a second stochastic process, v(t), following a mean-reverting SDE correlated with the stock's own Brownian motion, using the multivariate Ito framework from the previous lesson.

Its four parameters, κ, θ, ξ, and ρ, control mean-reversion speed, long-run variance, volatility-of-volatility, and the leverage effect (typically negative for equities, matching the real Nifty-VIX inverse relationship).
Simulating v(t) safely requires a numerical safeguard, full truncation, since naive discretization can otherwise produce a negative, meaningless variance.

Pricing options rigorously under Heston needs Fourier-based methods beyond this course's scope; the next lesson addresses a different broken assumption entirely, continuity, with a model built to handle sudden market gaps.
